title: Reading a reinforcement-learning optimizer: where it walks, what it earns, and what it may claim
summary: Eight Playground figures follow an agent that tunes model weights by reinforcement learning: its path through a 2D slice of weight space, the objective and reward over training, the size of its actions, the autocorrelation of its reward, and a matched-budget comparison with two classical optimizers that ends in a verdict. Each tells you something different about whether the agent is learning or wandering.

media.alt: A dark scatter plot titled weight-space trajectory with a fixed random 2D projection. Several hundred small dots joined by thin lines wander through projected dimension one from minus two to nine and dimension two from minus five to two. Colour runs from dark purple at early steps to yellow at step 400; a red star marks the start.

read_the_figure.question: Is the agent making progress, exploring, or stuck, and is the comparison with other optimizers fair?
read_the_figure.axes: Trajectory: projected dimension 1 and 2 of the weights (a fixed random projection), colour is the step number up to 400. Objective figure: step on the horizontal axis; top, the loss on a log scale and the running minimum; bottom, the reward (loss decrease) per step. Action figure: fraction of the episode elapsed against the size of the projected action. Autocorrelation: lag in steps against correlation. Scorecard and verdict: bars and text for each backend at one budget.
look_at: Trajectory: the path starts at the red star, wanders through the left cloud (purple to blue), jumps right (green), and finishes in a yellow cluster. Large jumps and small clusters suggest alternating exploration and local search; a 2D projection hides most of the weight space, so distances in the picture are not distances in the model.

Objective: the running minimum (green, bottom curve in the top panel) falls in the first few tens of steps and then stays flat for the rest of the 400. The raw loss (blue) swings over four decades, then drifts upward. A flat running minimum means no new best was found, not that the optimizer converged.

Reward: bars above zero are loss decreases, below zero are increases. They are roughly symmetric with a few very large spikes near steps 200 to 215, so the sum of rewards is dominated by a handful of steps.
Action versus phase: the binned mean of the action size is nearly flat across the episode, so the agent has not learned to take smaller steps as it nears the end.

Autocorrelation: lag 0 is 1 by definition. Lag 1 is negative, about -0.3, and the rest scatter within +-0.2, which is mostly noise. A value near -0.5 at lag 1 is what a reward made of differences of independent losses gives.

Scorecard and verdict: three backends at a matched budget of 400 evaluations; the verdict states criteria declared before reading results and limits its claim to this problem and these backends. The numbers on those two figures are not reproduced here.
read_the_figure.proves: A comparison at matched budget with a pre-declared threshold is the minimum for a fair verdict. The diagnostics show how the agent behaves on the way: early progress then a plateau, noisy rewards, no learned step schedule.
if_wrong: A flat running minimum from step 20 onwards: the remaining budget bought nothing; compare with the baselines at their first-20-step values.
A reward dominated by a few spikes: seed-to-seed variation will be large; one run is not evidence.
A trajectory that never settles: the projection may hide the structure, or the agent is still exploring.
A verdict without declared criteria or scope: it is a story, not a test.
must_check: That the budget (here 400 evaluations) is the same for every backend.
That the success threshold was fixed before the results (the verdict says it was).
That the number of seeds is stated; here a single run is shown.
That the projection used for the trajectory is fixed, not refit per step, and its limits are noted.

terms.meaning: In reinforcement learning an agent picks an action in a state and receives a reward.
Proximal policy optimization: a policy-gradient method that limits how far each update moves the policy.
The path of the model's parameters over training, shown in a 2D projection.
The minimum objective found so far; it can only go down.
Correlation of a signal with itself at a lag of k steps.
Every method gets the same number of objective evaluations.
A threshold fixed before looking at results, so that the verdict cannot be tuned to the outcome.

remember: The reward here is the decrease in loss, so the total reward over an episode telescopes to the total improvement.
A running best is monotone; a plateau means no improvement, which is not the same as convergence.
Autocorrelation at lag 1 of a difference of independent noisy values is -0.5.
Compare optimizers at equal budget, over several seeds, with a threshold fixed in advance.
A 2D projection of weights loses most of the geometry.

steps.title: Reward as a loss decrease telescopes
steps.note: So the return is the net improvement over the episode. The few huge bars in the reward panel mostly cancel: a big gain followed by a big loss nets to little.

steps.title: Why lag-1 autocorrelation is negative
steps.note: If the loss at each step were an independent random draw, the reward would have exactly this lag-1 correlation. The observed value (about -0.3) means part of the loss movement is noise and part is structure.

steps.title: Running best
steps.note: The green curve is this. Its flat tail says that no step after about the twentieth beat the best loss found, which is a statement about the search, not a proof of an optimum.

steps.title: The PPO clipped objective
steps.note: The clip stops one update from changing the policy too much. It is the standard published form and is all this explainer asserts about the agent.

steps.title: A pre-declared competitiveness rule
steps.note: R is the ratio of the agent's best objective to the best of the comparison backends at equal budget; R_max is fixed before the run. With illustrative numbers 2.1 and 1.9, R = 1.1.

worked.title: Autocorrelation of a reward made of differences
worked.problem: Simulate independent losses f_t and form r_t = f_t - f_{t+1}. What lag-1 autocorrelation do you get, and how does it compare with the figure?
worked.answer: -0.5. The figure shows about -0.3, so the agent's rewards are less anti-correlated than pure noise would give: some of its loss changes are persistent.

analyze.q: The running minimum is flat from about step 20 to 400. Give two readings (optimum found, search stuck) and one experiment that distinguishes them.
analyze.hint: Restart from a different start or seed.

analyze.q: Why can reward spikes near step 200 matter little for the final objective?
The action size is flat over the episode. What would a learned annealing schedule look like in this panel?

evaluate.q: Is a matched budget of 400 evaluations enough to say 'RL is competitive with classical solvers'? What are the limits stated in the verdict figure?
evaluate.hint: One problem, own backends, first-pass settings.

evaluate.q: What would turn the verdict from a single-run statement into one you would trust?
evaluate.hint: Seeds, several problems, an interval on R.

create: Write the criteria card you would declare before running a comparison of the agent with two classical solvers: budget, seeds, threshold, scope.
Design a trajectory plot whose projection axes are the two directions of largest variance of the visited weights and compare its readability with the random projection.

checks.answer: The decrease in loss from one step to the next; negative when the loss went up.

checks.q: Rewards over three steps are +4, -1, +2. Total improvement?
checks.answer: +5: the loss fell by 5 in total.

checks.q: Why is the lag-1 autocorrelation of a reward made of loss differences expected to be negative?
checks.answer: Consecutive rewards share the same loss value with opposite sign (r_t has -f_{t+1}, r_{t+1} has +f_{t+1}), which gives -0.5 for independent noise.

checks.q: The verdict says ADOPT with a ratio inside a threshold. What does it not say?
checks.answer: It makes no general claim about reinforcement learning versus optimization: one problem, the repository's own CMA and Nelder-Mead backends, one budget.

checks.q: Add one panel that would test whether the agent exploits local loss structure.
checks.answer: Plot the same autocorrelation for a random-action policy and overlay it; a difference at lag 1 to 3 would indicate exploitation.
